output.normalized_title: search-indexer: DNS resolution timeout on route53 (search-indexer)

output.classification_reasoning: The incident is centered on a DNS resolution timeout when querying Route53, which is a clear network‑level symptom rather than an application or data store error. DNS failures propagate to the search-indexer service, causing telemetry spikes and user impact. Resolving the issue requires investigating external DNS infrastructure, route propagation, and potential VPC/DNS resolver configurations, which involves multiple network components and dependencies. This breadth of investigation places the incident above a simple one‑step fix but does not require deep multi‑service orchestration, thus it is classified as moderately complex.

prerequisites: Root access or AWS SSO role ProdOperations
output.security_notes: Do not terminate the primary node without first promoting a read‑replica. Verify that a write‑freeze is in place before any node reboot or termination.

diagnostic_stage_assessment.notes: Current DNS timeout mirrors INC-1003 which affected redis-cluster; suggests a similar network/DNS issue now impacting search-indexer.

output.justification: The incident affects 800 users, well above the 100‑user threshold for a moderate disruption. The outage duration is 31 minutes, which exceeds the Tier‑3 SLA tolerance for moderate incidents (typically up to 30 minutes before escalation). The correlated context shows a recurring network/DNS failure pattern that aligns with previous moderate‑severity incidents (INC-1003). With a confidence score of 0.78 in root‑cause identification and impact on critical services (redis-cluster, search-indexer), the deterministic rule correctly recommends SEV-3.

remediation_steps.title: Validate Operator Access and Kubernetes Context
remediation_steps.description: Ensure the engineer has the required ProdOperations role and that kubectl is pointed at the production cluster.
verification: AWS identity ARN matches ProdOperations role
kubectl context string contains 'prod-us-east-1'
Master node list is reachable

remediation_steps.title: Confirm DNS Resolution for Affected Services
remediation_steps.description: Diagnose the Route53 DNS timeout by querying the service records directly from a pod inside the cluster.
commands: kubectl run dns-test --rm -i --tty --image=busybox -- /bin/sh -c "nslookup search-indexer.internal && nslookup redis-cluster.internal"
verification: Both nslookup commands return a valid IP address within 2 seconds
No 'SERVFAIL' or timeout errors observed

remediation_steps.title: Apply Corrective Route53 Record Update
remediation_steps.description: If DNS lookup failed, update the affected A/AAAA records or health checks in Route53. Ensure a write‑freeze is in place before any primary node changes.
verification: aws route53 get-change --id <change-id> returns status 'INSYNC'
Re‑run step 2 commands and observe successful resolution

remediation_steps.title: Promote Redis Read‑Replica (if primary is impacted)
remediation_steps.description: Before any node reboot, promote a healthy read‑replica to become the new primary to preserve data availability.
commands: kubectl exec -n redis redis-cluster-0 -- redis-cli -h <old-primary> CLUSTER FAILOVER TAKEOVER
kubectl get pods -n redis -l app=redis-cluster -o wide
verification: New primary reports role 'master' in `redis-cli INFO replication`
Application pods report successful connection to Redis without errors

remediation_steps.title: Perform Rolling Restart of Search‑Indexer Deployment
remediation_steps.description: Gracefully restart the search-indexer pods to pick up the corrected DNS configuration and clear any stale connections.
verification: All pods reach READY=1/1 and STATUS=Running
curl -sSf https://search-indexer.internal/healthz returns HTTP 200 with body 'OK'

remediation_steps.title: Post‑Remediation Health Audit
remediation_steps.description: Validate end‑to‑end service health, error rates, and user impact.
commands: kubectl logs -l app=search-indexer --since=5m | grep ERR_NETWORK_FAILURE_370 || true
verification: Both health endpoints return HTTP 200 and 'OK'
Log grep returns no matching error signatures
Monitoring dashboards show <5% error rate for affected services

rollback_plan.overall_strategy: Revert any DNS record changes, demote the promoted Redis replica back to read‑only, and undo the search‑indexer rollout to the previous image tag. Each action includes verification before proceeding to the next.

steps.title: Revert Route53 Record Changes
steps.description: Restore the original DNS record set using the previously exported configuration.
verification: aws route53 get-change --id <rollback-change-id> returns status 'INSYNC'
Re‑run DNS validation (step 2) and confirm original records resolve

steps.title: Demote Redis Primary Back to Read‑Replica (if promoted)
steps.description: If the previous primary is healthy, revert the failover by promoting it back and setting the temporary primary to replica mode.
commands: kubectl exec -n redis redis-cluster-new-primary-0 -- redis-cli -h <new-primary> CLUSTER REPLICATE <old-primary-id>
kubectl exec -n redis redis-cluster-old-primary-0 -- redis-cli -h <old-primary> CLUSTER FAILOVER TAKEOVER
verification: Old primary reports role 'master' in `redis-cli INFO replication`
New primary reports role 'slave'
Application connectivity tests succeed

steps.title: Undo Search‑Indexer Deployment Rollout
steps.description: Revert the deployment to the previous container image tag.
verification: Pods are running the previous image tag (verify with `kubectl get pod -l app=search-indexer -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}'`)
Health endpoint returns HTTP 200
No resurgence of DNS‑related errors in logs

prerequisite_checks: All rollback commands reviewed and approved by change advisory board
safety_verification.notes: All actions are reversible, include verification checkpoints, and respect the security note to never terminate the primary node without promotion.
